profilePeriod: Labour leadership and government, 1935–1955, incorporating explicitly dated later votes and statements through October 1965

sources.title: History of Clement Attlee, UK Government
sources.evidence: Government nationalised coal, electricity and transport, introduced NHS and social insurance, passed planning and national-parks legislation, and decolonised India, Pakistan, Burma, Ceylon and Jordan. Leadership 1935–1955; premiership 1945–1951.

sources.title: Let Us Face the Future, Labour manifesto
sources.evidence: Programme defended press, speech, worship and trade-union freedoms; planned investment and rent/necessity price controls; redistribution and full employment; modern science and productive industry. This is collective party policy under Attlee, not his sole-authored text.

sources.title: Welsh Affairs: government statement by Herbert Morrison
sources.evidence: Government announced nominated, advisory Council for Wales; rejected ministerial chairmanship and preserved Westminster parliamentary authority. The council was consultative, not a devolved legislature.

sources.title: House of Commons briefing, Referendums
sources.evidence: Attlee rejected Churchill’s proposal for a referendum to prolong the wartime coalition and postpone the general election, defending representative parliamentary elections.

sources.title: Civil Service (Communists and Fascists), Hansard
sources.evidence: Government defended excluding communists and fascists from sensitive civil-service work on national-security grounds, with review arrangements, rather than prohibiting their political parties.

sources.title: Communist Party, Great Britain, Hansard
sources.evidence: Attlee explicitly refused to introduce legislation outlawing the British Communist Party after the Fuchs espionage trial.

sources.title: Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Bill division
sources.evidence: Attlee voted Not-Content against an amendment retaining capital punishment for murders associated with police/prison-officer protection and arrest. Later public vote included under the explicit profile period.

sources.title: Attlee letter on Windrush, National Archives
sources.evidence: Attlee defended free admission of British subjects irrespective of race or colour, citing Commonwealth loyalty and tradition, while downplaying expectations of continued large-scale arrival. This was Commonwealth citizenship, not universal open borders.

sources.title: Decision to build a British atomic bomb, FCDO history
sources.evidence: Attlee’s ministerial committee authorised a domestic atomic-bomb programme for security and strategic independence despite economic cost.

sources.title: Attlee to Chifley, Australian diplomatic archive
sources.evidence: Attlee advocated military standardisation and defence research cooperation with the United States and Canada, preserving Commonwealth strength; he distinguished this stage from a formal alliance.

sources.title: Malayan Emergency, National Army Museum
sources.evidence: The 1950 Briggs strategy coordinated military and police action and controlled settlement populations; by end 1951 hundreds of thousands had been resettled. Later Templer-era acts are excluded from Attlee attribution.

sources.title: Who owns the Bank of England?
sources.evidence: The Bank became publicly owned in 1946. Use nationalisation as evidence of public monetary authority; do not import its later operational independence into Attlee’s period.

sources.title: WTO history of the 1947 GATT negotiations
sources.evidence: UK participation in GATT tariff negotiations coexisted with retention, but not enlargement, of imperial tariff-preference margins. Negotiated liberalisation was compatible with selective protection.

sources.title: Clement Attlee, Humanist Heritage
sources.evidence: Attlee did not believe in God; valued Christian ethical inheritance and respected believers. Secular motivation did not amount to militant antireligion.

sources.title: Education Act 1944, National Archives
sources.evidence: Coalition education settlement retained denominational participation and a religious settlement. Attlee’s subsequent government implemented this framework; source is contextual, not an Attlee personal declaration.

sources.title: Sexual Offences Bill, Attlee speech and division
sources.evidence: Attlee supported reversal of the Labouchere provision but endorsed Dilhorne’s amendment retaining criminalisation of sodomy; partial liberalisation coexisted with restrictive morality.

sources.title: Sexual Offences Bill, Attlee speech
sources.evidence: Attlee defended reform on grounds that the law failed to deter and should accord with justice, while describing homosexual conduct negatively. Distinguish legal reform from moral endorsement or present-day LGBT equality.

sources.title: Equal Pay (Government Policy), Hansard
sources.evidence: Attlee affirmed governmental acceptance of equal pay in principle while retaining qualifications over practical implementation.

sources.title: National Health Service Bill debate
sources.evidence: Contemporary debate records that the government NHS Bill abolished compulsory vaccination; supports distinguishing public provision from blanket medical coercion. Criticism is by a parliamentary opponent, not an Attlee quotation.

sources.title: National Library of Ireland catalogue: The Labour party in perspective
sources.evidence: Catalogue records C. R. Attlee as author, Victor Gollancz, London, 1937; subject Labour Party/socialism. A direct political book, selected over his broader memoir.

sources.title: Museu do Ouro library catalogue
sources.evidence: Brazilian museum lists Clement Attlee, Bases e Fundamentos do Trabalhismo, Rio de Janeiro, Editora A Noite, Imagens da Época 2.

sources.title: University of Brasília dissertation bibliography/context
sources.date: Dissertation; discusses 1937 book and 1955 Brazilian edition
sources.evidence: Explicitly links The Labour Party in Perspective, first issued 1937, with Brazilian Bases e Fundamentos do Trabalhismo. Brazilian edition dates vary in bibliographies; entry year is original 1937, not translation date.

facts: 1946 NHS and nationalised infrastructure used central standards and national institutions.
1948 Welsh advisory council preserved Westminster law-making; municipal administration remained meaningful.
estrutura.tension: Unitary parliamentary government did not entail abolishing local government; colonial independence is not domestic federalism.

facts: 1945 manifesto defended civil freedoms and elected socialist reform.
Attlee rejected the 1945 referendum proposal and maintained parliamentary elections; refused to outlaw communists in 1950.
representacao.tension: Strong representative democracy, without endorsing plebiscites, leaderless assemblies or unelected constitutional supremacy over Parliament.

facts: 1948 security screening limited sensitive employment.
1950 refusal to ban communists and 1965 anti-retention capital-punishment vote limit an authoritarian reading.
1946 NHS Bill rejected compulsory vaccination; Malayan emergency used coercive population control.
poder.tension: Domestic liberties and later penal reform coexist with emergency powers and imperial coercion; public healthcare is not automatic blanket compulsion.

facts: 1948 Windrush letter defended Commonwealth-subject entry regardless of colour, alongside concern to preserve Commonwealth loyalty.
imigracao.tension: Neither a racial exclusion programme nor modern universal open-border multiculturalism; practical integration and citizenship boundaries matter.

facts: 1947 atomic-bomb decision and defence cooperation demonstrate material armament commitment.
Labour rejected Nazi aggression and maintained overseas force.
diplomacia.tension: Defence and deterrence with allies, not enthusiasm for war for its own sake or pacifist disarmament.

facts: Independence for several colonies coexisted with intervention in Malaya.
1947 Attlee letter sought Western/Commonwealth military coordination.
intervencao.tension: Anti-isolationist and willing to defend influence, while accepting negotiated self-government; decolonisation does not imply no foreign deployment.

facts: NHS, national insurance, nationalisation of coal, electricity and transport enacted 1946–1948.
Government preserved a large private sector; programme used constitutional reform and unions.
economia.tension: Public strategic sectors and welfare are central; do not infer elimination of all firms or revolutionary expropriation.

facts: 1945 programme explicitly planned investment and controlled essential prices/rents.
1946 nationalisation of central bank supports elected direction of monetary institutions.
controle.tension: Extensive direction of a mixed economy, not necessarily comprehensive state planning of every transaction.

facts: 1947 GATT negotiations expanded reciprocal trade while retaining imperial preferences.
comercio.tension: Support trade expansion and negotiated reductions; reject both complete autarky and unconditional zero tariffs/capital freedom.

facts: Personal unbelief coexisted with respect for Christian social ethics.
1944 education settlement and freedom of worship remained compatible with his government.
religiao.tension: Secular ethical politics without suppression of religion or automatic removal of every religious custom.

facts: 1950 equal-pay principle with implementation qualifications.
June 1965 supported limited homosexual-law reform with retained restrictions; October 1965 justified reform pragmatically while morally disapproving.
moral.tension: Do not import contemporary identity politics or equate reform of criminal law with same-sex marriage/adoption endorsement. Family norms remain cautious.

facts: 1945 programme championed science, modern homes and industrial productivity.
1947 atomic programme demonstrates technological ambition; 1949 National Parks and planning constrain development.
tecnologia.tension: Industrial modernisation plus public regulation and conservation; no evidence for transhumanism or unrestricted enhancement.

limitations: Modern Brazilian institutions are interpreted functionally; references to Brazil become Britain or analogous national decisions, never claims that Attlee discussed Brazil’s present policies.
AI, crypto, facial recognition, gene editing, modern gender language and laboratory meat answers are explicitly analogical judgements from documented principles, not recovered statements.
Government or party programmes are collective evidence and are labelled separately from personal speeches/votes.
Historical model retains 1935–1955 leadership plus explicitly dated public evidence through October 1965. Later acts by successors, private conjectures and posthumous norms excluded.
Technology and contemporary family-policy extrapolations have lower confidence; N is reserved for substantive conflict, not missing evidence.

recommendedMetadata.reason: Both PT and EN accurately capture government period, nationalisation, NHS, decolonisation, NATO and nuclear/military commitments; existing names and roles accurate.

bookDecision.reason: Self-authored political exposition; relevant to parliamentary-socialist doctrine. No existing books.json entry. Verified original 1937 and actual Brazilian title, rather than translating title ad hoc.

likelyNeighboursAndDistinctions: Fabian and democratic-socialist neighbours: shared parliamentary public provision; Attlee is distinguished by actual nationalisation and NHS construction, early Cold War defence and imperial emergencies.
Keynesian/social-liberal neighbours: shared demand management and constitutional politics, but Attlee accepted broader state ownership and labour organisation.
Communist neighbours: shared planning language does not imply one-party rule, wholesale collectivisation, or religious repression.
Conservative Atlanticist neighbours: shared defence alliances and cautious family norms, but sharply different ownership, welfare and trade-union policies.
